questions.prompt: One of these is an example of extensive physical property
questions.explanation: Volume depends on the amount of sample, so it is extensive. Density, solubility and colour do not.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an intensive physical property?
questions.explanation: Density does not change when you take a larger sample of the same material.

questions.prompt: Which pair are both extensive properties?
questions.explanation: Mass and volume both increase when the sample is larger.

questions.prompt: A drop of pure water and a litre of pure water have the same
questions.explanation: Boiling point is intensive, so both samples boil at 100 °C at 1 atm.

questions.prompt: An example of chemical property is
questions.explanation: Rusting makes a new substance (iron oxide). Solubility, conductivity and melting are physical.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a physical property?
questions.explanation: Melting point does not make a new substance.

questions.prompt: Burning of paper is a chemical change because
options: a new substance (ash and gas) is formed
questions.explanation: Ash and gases are new substances, so burning is chemical.

questions.prompt: Which change is chemical?
questions.explanation: Rust is a new compound. The other three are physical.

questions.prompt: Which one is not true about pure substance?
questions.explanation: A pure substance has fixed melting point, boiling point and density. Volume depends on how much sample you take, so it is not a fixed characteristic.

questions.prompt: A pure substance can be identified by its
options: changing density from drop to drop
questions.explanation: A pure substance has a sharp, fixed melting point.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a mixture is true?
options: It has a fixed boiling point
questions.explanation: A mixture has a variable composition. Pure substances have fixed composition.

questions.prompt: Distilled water is a pure substance because it has
options: a fixed boiling point of 100 °C at 1 atm
questions.explanation: Pure water boils at 100 °C at 1 atm. That fixed BP shows it is pure.

questions.prompt: The chemical symbol of the potassium element is
questions.explanation: Potassium takes its symbol K from the Latin name kalium.

questions.prompt: The chemical symbol of sodium is
questions.explanation: Sodium takes Na from the Latin name natrium.

questions.prompt: The chemical symbol P stands for
questions.explanation: P is phosphorus. Potassium is K and platinum is Pt.

questions.prompt: The chemical symbol of iron is
questions.explanation: Iron takes Fe from the Latin name ferrum.

questions.prompt: The second most abundant element in human body is
questions.explanation: By mass, the human body is about 65% oxygen, then about 18% carbon. Silicon and aluminium are common in Earth's crust, not in the body.

questions.prompt: The most abundant element in the human body by mass is
questions.explanation: Oxygen is about 65% of body mass, mainly in water.

questions.prompt: The second most abundant element in Earth's crust is
questions.explanation: Earth's crust is about 47% oxygen and 28% silicon.

questions.prompt: Which element is a major building block of proteins and nucleic acids but is only about 3% of body mass?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen is the fourth most abundant body element and is found in proteins and DNA.

questions.prompt: Which one is true for the homogenous mixture?
options: Components can be identified by our naked eye
questions.explanation: A homogeneous mixture is uniform throughout. You cannot see separate parts, and it has one phase.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a homogeneous mixture?
questions.explanation: Sugar water is uniform. The others show more than one part.

questions.prompt: A heterogeneous mixture
options: has parts you can tell apart
questions.explanation: Heterogeneous mixtures have visibly different parts or more than one phase.

questions.prompt: Air (with no dust or mist) is best classified as a
questions.explanation: Clean air is a uniform mixture of gases, so it is homogeneous.

questions.prompt: Salt can be separated from sea water by using a method of
questions.explanation: Evaporation drives off the water and leaves the salt. Grade 9 texts teach evaporation as the method to obtain salt from seawater.

questions.prompt: Pure water can be obtained from seawater by
questions.explanation: Distillation boils the water and condenses the vapour, leaving salt behind.

questions.prompt: Sand is separated from a sand–water mixture by
questions.explanation: Sand is an undissolved solid, so it is trapped by a filter.

questions.prompt: Iodine crystals mixed with sand are best separated by
questions.explanation: Iodine sublimes on heating and can be collected as a solid again on a cold surface.

questions.prompt: One of these is not a property of a metal
questions.explanation: Metals are typically malleable, ductile and lustrous. Soft and brittle describes most non-metals.

questions.prompt: A metal that can be drawn into a wire is described as
questions.explanation: Ductility is the ability to be drawn into a wire.

questions.prompt: Which property is typical of a non-metal such as sulfur?
questions.explanation: Solid non-metals are usually brittle and dull.

questions.prompt: Metals are good conductors of heat and electricity because they have
questions.explanation: Free (delocalised) electrons carry charge and heat through the metal.

questions.prompt: Mass number of an atom is the sum of number of ______ and ______.
questions.explanation: Mass number A = protons + neutrons (the nucleons).

questions.prompt: The atomic number of an atom is the number of
questions.explanation: Atomic number Z is the number of protons.

questions.prompt: Nucleons are
questions.explanation: Nucleons are the particles in the nucleus: protons and neutrons.

questions.prompt: Two isotopes of the same element have the same number of ______ but different numbers of ______.
questions.explanation: Isotopes have the same Z (protons) and different N (neutrons), so different A.

questions.prompt: An atom has atomic number 13 and mass number 27. Then the number of neutrons is equal to
questions.explanation: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 27 − 13 = 14.

questions.prompt: An atom has atomic number 11 and mass number 23. How many neutrons does it have?
A neutral atom has 17 protons and 18 neutrons. Its mass number is
questions.explanation: A = protons + neutrons = 17 + 18 = 35.

questions.prompt: Carbon-14 has atomic number 6. The number of neutrons is
The third shell of an atom contains a maximum of __________ electrons
questions.explanation: The third shell is n = 3, so the maximum is 2n² = 2 × 9 = 18 electrons.

questions.prompt: The second shell of an atom contains a maximum of how many electrons?
The first shell of an atom contains a maximum of how many electrons?
The fourth shell of an atom contains a maximum of how many electrons?
The maximum number of electrons in a shell is determined by the formula
questions.explanation: The Bohr rule is 2n², where n is the shell number.

questions.prompt: Using 2n², the maximum electrons in shell n = 5 is
Which calculation is correct for the L-shell (n = 2)?
questions.explanation: L-shell maximum is 8, from 2n² = 2×4.

questions.prompt: If a student uses (2n)² instead of 2n² for n = 3, the wrong maximum they get is
questions.explanation: (2×3)² = 6² = 36, but the true maximum is 18.

questions.prompt: An atom is electrically neutral because of having equal number of
questions.explanation: Protons are positive and electrons are negative. Equal numbers cancel, so the atom is neutral.

questions.prompt: A positive ion (cation) is formed when an atom
questions.explanation: Losing electrons leaves more protons than electrons, so the ion is positive.

questions.prompt: A chloride ion Cl⁻ has 17 protons. How many electrons does it have?
questions.explanation: The extra negative charge means one extra electron: 17 + 1 = 18.

questions.prompt: Neutrons do not affect the charge of an atom because they
questions.explanation: A neutron is electrically neutral.

questions.prompt: The element phosphorus has atomic number 15. This atom has valence electrons
questions.explanation: Phosphorus is 2, 8, 5. The outer shell has 5 electrons, so it has 5 valence electrons.

questions.prompt: Oxygen has atomic number 8. How many valence electrons does it have?
questions.explanation: Oxygen is 2, 6 so it has 6 valence electrons.

questions.prompt: Sodium has atomic number 11. The number of valence electrons is
questions.explanation: Sodium is 2, 8, 1 so it has 1 valence electron.

questions.prompt: An element has electron arrangement 2, 8, 7. How many valence electrons does it have?
questions.explanation: The outer number is 7, so there are 7 valence electrons (chlorine).

questions.prompt: Which of these shells has the lowest energy?
questions.explanation: The K-shell is closest to the nucleus (n = 1) and has the lowest energy.

questions.prompt: Which shell has the highest energy among K, L, M and N?
questions.explanation: N is n = 4, farthest of these four, so it has the highest energy.

questions.prompt: Electrons fill shells in the order of
questions.explanation: The Aufbau idea at Grade 9 is: fill the lowest energy shell first (K, then L, then M).

questions.prompt: The L-shell is the
Which of the following is not a correct name–symbol combination?
questions.explanation: Manganese is Mn. Mg is magnesium.

questions.prompt: The symbol for manganese is
questions.explanation: Mn is manganese.

questions.prompt: Mg is the symbol for
questions.explanation: Mg = magnesium.

questions.prompt: The symbol Na stands for
questions.explanation: Na from natrium.

questions.prompt: Positively charged ions are called
questions.explanation: Cations are positive. Anions are negative.

questions.prompt: Negatively charged ions are called
questions.explanation: Anion = negative.

questions.prompt: Na⁺ is a
questions.explanation: Sodium ion is positive.

questions.prompt: Cl⁻ is a
questions.explanation: Chloride is negative.

questions.prompt: An element X with 2 valence electrons reacts with an element Y that has 6 valence electrons. A possible formula for the resulting compound is
questions.explanation: X tends to form X²⁺ (lose 2). Y tends to form Y²⁻ (gain 2). The 1:1 compound is XY.

questions.prompt: Mg (2 valence) and O (6 valence) form
questions.explanation: Mg²⁺ O²⁻ → MgO.

questions.prompt: An atom that loses 2 electrons becomes
questions.explanation: Loss of electrons → cation.

questions.prompt: An atom with 6 valence electrons commonly forms
questions.explanation: Needs 2 more electrons for an octet.

questions.prompt: Choose the pair of names and formulas that do not match
questions.explanation: Sodium sulfate is Na₂SO₄, not Na₂S. Na₂S is sodium sulfide, which is option D and is correctly paired.

questions.prompt: The formula of sodium sulfate is
questions.explanation: Two Na⁺ and one SO₄²⁻.

questions.prompt: Na₂S is named
questions.explanation: S²⁻ is sulfide.

questions.prompt: CaF₂ is
questions.explanation: Ca²⁺ and 2 F⁻.

questions.prompt: If a metallic element M forms an ion M³⁺, what will be the formula of the metal sulfate?
questions.explanation: M³⁺ and SO₄²⁻ criss-cross to M₂(SO₄)₃.

questions.prompt: Aluminium sulfate is
questions.explanation: Al³⁺ and SO₄²⁻ → Al₂(SO₄)₃.

questions.prompt: Fe³⁺ with Cl⁻ gives
questions.explanation: One Fe³⁺ needs three Cl⁻.

questions.prompt: The sulfate ion is
questions.explanation: Sulfate = SO₄²⁻.

questions.prompt: The formula for the sulfite ion is
questions.explanation: Sulfite is SO₃²⁻. Sulfate is SO₄²⁻. Sulfide is S²⁻. Thiosulfate is S₂O₃²⁻.

questions.prompt: The sulfate ion is
questions.explanation: Sulfate has four oxygens.

questions.prompt: S²⁻ is the
questions.explanation: Simple sulfide.

questions.prompt: How many oxygen atoms are in one sulfite ion?
questions.explanation: SO₃²⁻ has three O.

questions.prompt: If the empirical formula of a compound is CH₃ and its molecular mass is 45, what is the molecular formula?
questions.explanation: CH₃ has mass 15. 45/15 = 3, so C₃H₉.

questions.prompt: The empirical-formula mass of CH₃ is
If empirical CH and M=78, the molecular formula is
questions.explanation: CH mass 13. 78/13=6 → C₆H₆.

questions.prompt: C₂H₆ has empirical formula
questions.explanation: Divide by 2.

questions.prompt: When two compounds react to form two other compounds the reaction type is called
questions.explanation: AB + CD → AD + CB is double replacement (double displacement).

questions.prompt: A + B → AB is
questions.explanation: Two become one.

questions.prompt: AB → A + B is
questions.explanation: One becomes two.

questions.prompt: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O is
questions.explanation: Burning in oxygen is combustion.

questions.prompt: If the molecular formula of the compound is C₆H₁₂O₆, what is the empirical formula?
questions.explanation: Divide C₆H₁₂O₆ by 6 to get CH₂O, the simplest ratio.

questions.prompt: The empirical formula of C₂H₆ is
questions.explanation: Divide by 2.

questions.prompt: CH₂O is the empirical formula of
questions.explanation: Glucose reduces to CH₂O.

questions.prompt: C₃H₆O₃ simplified fully is
questions.explanation: Divide by 3.

questions.prompt: Matter is defined as anything that
options: has mass and takes up space
questions.explanation: The Grade 9 definition: matter is anything that has mass and occupies space. Light, sound and ideas are not matter.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is matter?
questions.explanation: Steam is water vapour: it has mass and volume. Light, sound and heat are forms of energy.

questions.prompt: A gas is matter because it
questions.explanation: A gas fills its container (volume) and can be weighed (mass), so it is matter.

questions.prompt: Which statement about matter is correct?
options: It is only found as a solid
questions.explanation: Mass and volume are the two properties that define matter, in any of the three common states.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is not matter?
questions.explanation: Steam, alcohol and milk all have mass and volume. A sound wave is a travelling vibration (energy), so it is not matter.

questions.prompt: Which of these is not matter?
questions.explanation: Light is electromagnetic radiation, not a substance with rest mass.

questions.prompt: A radio wave is
questions.explanation: Radio waves are electromagnetic waves, so they are energy, not matter.

questions.prompt: Milk is classified as matter because it
questions.explanation: Colour and origin are not the definition. Milk can be poured into a volume and weighed.

questions.prompt: Which physical state has a definite volume?
questions.explanation: Solids and liquids have a fixed volume. A gas has neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume; it fills the container.

questions.prompt: A gas has
options: neither definite shape nor definite volume
questions.explanation: Gas particles fill any container, so both shape and volume change with the container.

questions.prompt: A liquid differs from a solid because a liquid
questions.explanation: Both have definite volume and mass. A liquid takes the shape of the lower part of its container.

questions.prompt: Which state of matter is the most compressible?
questions.explanation: Gas particles are far apart, so a gas can be squeezed into a much smaller volume.

questions.prompt: The temperature at which a substance is changed from liquid to solid is called the
questions.explanation: Freezing point is the temperature at which a liquid becomes a solid. For a pure substance it equals the melting point.

questions.prompt: The melting point is the temperature at which a substance changes from
questions.explanation: Melting is fusion: solid → liquid at the melting point.

questions.prompt: Boiling point is the temperature at which a liquid becomes a
questions.explanation: At the boiling point the vapour pressure equals atmospheric pressure and the liquid vaporises throughout.

questions.prompt: For a pure substance the freezing point is the same temperature as the
questions.explanation: Solid and liquid are in equilibrium at one temperature for a pure substance — called melting point or freezing point depending on the direction.

questions.prompt: The process of changing gases to liquids is called
questions.explanation: Condensation is gas → liquid. Evaporation and boiling are liquid → gas; freezing is liquid → solid; melting is solid → liquid.

questions.prompt: Evaporation is the change from
options: liquid to gas at the surface
questions.explanation: Evaporation can occur below the boiling point and only at the surface.

questions.prompt: The direct change of a solid to a gas is
questions.explanation: Iodine, dry ice and naphthalene sublime: solid ⇌ gas with no liquid seen.

questions.prompt: Steam changing to water droplets on a cold lid is
questions.explanation: Water vapour loses energy and becomes liquid — condensation.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an intensive property?
options: The amount of alcohol in a bottle of beer
The energy obtained from eating a banana
questions.explanation: Intensive properties do not depend on sample size (density, temperature, boiling point). Mass, amount and energy are extensive.

questions.prompt: Which property is extensive?
questions.explanation: Mass adds when samples are combined, so it is extensive.

questions.prompt: Boiling point is an intensive property because it
options: does not change with the amount of pure liquid
questions.explanation: 1 cm³ and 1 L of pure water both boil at 100 °C at 1 atm.

questions.prompt: Density is calculated as
questions.explanation: ρ = m/V. Because both m and V scale together, density is intensive.

questions.prompt: Each of the following is a list of elements except
questions.explanation: Brass is an alloy (mixture of metals) and sea water is a mixture. Carbon is an element, but the list as a whole is not 'elements only'.

questions.prompt: Brass is
options: a compound of one metal only
questions.explanation: Brass is copper plus zinc, mixed, not chemically combined in a fixed ratio.

questions.prompt: Sea water is best classified as a
questions.explanation: Sea water contains water, salts, gases and other dissolved substances.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an element?
questions.explanation: Oxygen is element 8. Brass, air and sea water are mixtures.

questions.prompt: A separation technique used to separate a mixture of miscible liquids which have a boiling-point difference of at least 20 °C is
questions.explanation: Simple distillation separates miscible liquids whose boiling points differ by about 20 °C or more. Filtration and sedimentation need an insoluble solid; evaporation leaves a dissolved solid behind.

questions.prompt: Filtration separates
options: an insoluble solid from a liquid
dissolved salt from water only by itself
questions.explanation: The liquid (filtrate) passes through; the solid (residue) stays on the paper.

questions.prompt: Two miscible liquids with very close boiling points are separated by
questions.explanation: A fractionating column gives many mini-distillations so liquids with close boiling points can be split.

questions.prompt: Evaporation is useful for recovering
options: a dissolved solid from a solution
a gas dissolved in another gas
questions.explanation: The solvent boils or evaporates away; the solute remains as crystals or powder.

questions.prompt: A negatively charged sub-atomic particle is the
questions.explanation: The electron has charge −1. The proton is +1; the neutron is 0. Nucleon means proton or neutron.

questions.prompt: A proton is
options: positively charged and in the nucleus
negatively charged and outside the nucleus
questions.explanation: Protons (charge +1, mass ≈ 1 u) sit in the nucleus with neutrons.

questions.prompt: The neutron has
questions.explanation: Neutrons are electrically neutral nuclear particles of mass ≈ 1 u.

questions.prompt: Nucleons are
questions.explanation: Nucleon is the common name for the particles that make up the nucleus.

questions.prompt: A neutral atom has
options: an equal number of electrons and protons
an equal number of protons and neutrons
an equal number of electrons and neutrons
an equal number of nucleons and electrons
questions.explanation: Charge balance requires proton number = electron number. Neutron number can differ (isotopes), so the other equalities are not required.

questions.prompt: An atom with 11 protons and 10 electrons is
questions.explanation: One extra proton vs electrons gives charge +1 (Na+).

questions.prompt: Isotopes of an element have the same number of
questions.explanation: Same Z (protons) defines the element; neutrons (and A) differ.

questions.prompt: A chloride ion Cl− has
questions.explanation: Cl has Z = 17. Cl− has 18 electrons, so charge −1.

questions.prompt: The maximum number of electrons that an M-shell (M-energy level) can hold is
questions.explanation: The nth shell holds at most 2n² electrons. K is n=1 (2), L is n=2 (8), M is n=3 (18), N is n=4 (32).

questions.prompt: The K-shell can hold a maximum of
questions.explanation: K is the first shell (n=1); 2(1)² = 2.

questions.prompt: The maximum number of electrons in a shell is given by
questions.explanation: Bohr–Bury rule: capacity of shell n is 2n².

questions.prompt: The L-shell is the
options: second shell and holds up to 8 electrons
first shell and holds up to 2 electrons
third shell and holds up to 18 electrons
fourth shell and holds up to 32 electrons
questions.explanation: Order of shells: K, L, M, N. L is n=2.

questions.prompt: Which of the following pairs is isoelectronic? (Atomic number: Ne=10, Ca=20, Ar=18, Mg=12, O=8)
questions.explanation: Isoelectronic species have the same number of electrons. Ar has 18. Ca²⁺ has 20−2=18. Ne has 10; Ca²⁺ has 18. Mg²⁺ has 10. O²⁻ has 10.

questions.prompt: Mg²⁺ (Z=12) has the same number of electrons as
questions.explanation: Mg²⁺ has 12−2=10 electrons, equal to neon.

questions.prompt: O²⁻ (Z=8) is isoelectronic with
questions.explanation: O²⁻ has 8+2=10 electrons, the same as neon.

questions.prompt: Isoelectronic species have the same number of
questions.explanation: The definition compares electron count, not nuclear charge.

questions.prompt: How many hydrogen atoms combine with one nitrogen atom to form a covalent compound? (N has 5 valence electrons; H has 1)
questions.explanation: Nitrogen needs 3 more electrons to complete an octet, so it forms three single covalent bonds in NH3. (The paper labelled N=14, which is the mass number; the atomic number of N is 7.)

questions.prompt: The covalent compound of nitrogen and hydrogen is
questions.explanation: Ammonia is NH3, three N–H single bonds and a lone pair on nitrogen.

questions.prompt: A hydrogen atom can form how many covalent bonds?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen has one electron and one vacancy, so it forms one single bond (H2, HCl, NH3, CH4, …).

questions.prompt: Carbon (4 valence electrons) forms how many covalent bonds in methane?
questions.explanation: Carbon shares four electrons to complete an octet, giving CH4.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is not true about ionic compounds?
options: they do not consist of ions
they are solids at room temperature
they have generally high melting and boiling points
they are good conductors of electricity when molten or dissolved in water
questions.explanation: Ionic compounds are made of ions. The other listed properties are the usual textbook description of ionic solids.

questions.prompt: Ionic compounds conduct electricity when
questions.explanation: Ions must be free to move. That happens in the melt or in aqueous solution, not in the rigid solid lattice.

questions.prompt: Ionic bonds typically form between
questions.explanation: The metal loses electrons (cation) and the non-metal gains them (anion).

questions.prompt: The high melting points of ionic compounds are due to
options: strong attraction between oppositely charged ions
weak van der Waals forces only
questions.explanation: A lot of energy is needed to separate the cation–anion lattice.

questions.prompt: True or false: In chemical changes, no new substance is formed.
questions.explanation: A chemical change produces new substance(s) with new properties. Physical changes do not.

questions.prompt: True or false: Melting of ice is a chemical change.
questions.explanation: Ice and water are the same substance (H2O). Only the state changes.

questions.prompt: True or false: Rusting of iron produces a new substance.
questions.explanation: Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide, different from iron.

questions.prompt: True or false: A chemical change can usually be reversed by simple physical means.
questions.explanation: Chemical changes generally need another chemical reaction to reverse; physical changes are often easy to reverse.

questions.prompt: True or false: A homogeneous mixture has only one phase.
questions.explanation: Homogeneous means uniform composition and a single phase (e.g. salt water, air, brass).

questions.prompt: True or false: A heterogeneous mixture has more than one visible phase.
questions.explanation: Oil + water, sand + water, and granite show more than one phase.

questions.prompt: True or false: Air is a homogeneous mixture of gases.
questions.explanation: Clean air is a single gaseous phase of N2, O2, Ar, CO2 and traces.

questions.prompt: True or false: Oil and water form a homogeneous mixture.
questions.explanation: They do not mix; two liquid layers remain (heterogeneous).

questions.prompt: True or false: Sedimentation and decantation can be used to separate the constituents of a homogeneous mixture.
questions.explanation: Sedimentation and decantation need an insoluble solid that settles. A homogeneous mixture has no such separate solid phase.

questions.prompt: True or false: Sedimentation can separate sand from water.
questions.explanation: Sand is insoluble and denser, so it settles and the water can be poured off.

questions.prompt: True or false: Salt dissolved in water can be recovered by decantation alone.
questions.explanation: The salt is in the same phase as the water. You must evaporate or distil.

questions.prompt: True or false: Decantation is pouring off a liquid from a settled solid.
questions.explanation: That is the definition of decanting after sedimentation.

questions.prompt: True or false: The building block of every matter is an atom.
questions.explanation: Grade 9 textbook: atoms are the smallest units of elements that make up matter (elements, compounds and the parts of mixtures).

questions.prompt: True or false: An atom is the smallest particle of an element that keeps the chemical identity of that element.
questions.explanation: Split an atom and you no longer have that element.

questions.prompt: True or false: A compound is made of atoms of two or more elements chemically combined.
questions.explanation: H2O, CO2 and NaCl are compounds; the elements are bonded in a fixed ratio.

questions.prompt: True or false: Molecules are always made of atoms of only one element.
questions.explanation: O2 and N2 are molecules of one element, but CO2 and H2O are molecules of compounds.

questions.prompt: True or false: The protons of an atom are distributed in the electron shells (energy levels).
questions.explanation: Protons (and neutrons) are in the nucleus. Electrons occupy the shells.

questions.prompt: True or false: Electrons occupy energy levels around the nucleus.
questions.explanation: That is the Bohr–Bury picture taught in Grade 9.

questions.prompt: True or false: The nucleus contains protons and neutrons.
questions.explanation: The dense positive centre is made of nucleons.

questions.prompt: True or false: Neutrons orbit in the electron shells.
questions.explanation: Neutrons stay in the nucleus; they are not extra-nuclear.

questions.prompt: True or false: Elements that have a complete valence shell (eight valence electrons) are called noble gases.
questions.explanation: Group 18 atoms have a full outer shell (He has 2; the rest have 8) and are called noble or inert gases.

questions.prompt: True or false: Helium has eight valence electrons.
questions.explanation: Helium’s only shell (K) is full with 2 electrons. The octet rule starts from n=2.

questions.prompt: True or false: Neon is a noble gas.
questions.explanation: Neon (Z=10) has configuration 2,8 and is Group 18.

questions.prompt: True or false: Noble gases usually form many stable ionic compounds at room temperature.
questions.explanation: A full outer shell means they have little tendency to lose, gain or share electrons.

questions.prompt: True or false: An ionic bond is formed between two metallic atoms.
questions.explanation: An ionic bond forms between a metal and a non-metal. Two metals form a metallic bond (or an alloy).

questions.prompt: True or false: NaCl is held together by an ionic bond.
questions.explanation: Sodium (metal) transfers an electron to chlorine (non-metal).

questions.prompt: True or false: A bond between two chlorine atoms is ionic.
questions.explanation: Cl2 is two non-metals sharing a pair of electrons (covalent).

questions.prompt: True or false: Metallic bonds are found in a piece of copper metal.
questions.explanation: Copper atoms share a sea of delocalised electrons — metallic bonding.
